prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map captures an inverted/steeply pitched egocentric viewpoint on a tiled outdoor terrace bounded by a curved glass railing and a green-walled building overhang, clearly separating foreground subjects from the distant background. In frames 1 and 2, a person seated on the ground to the upper-left stretching toward their feet is the brightest and nearest element at roughly 1.5–2 m (just outside the camera wearer's arm's reach, though their own hands reach their shoes), situated about 0.5–1 m beside an oval white planter/bench and a small round stool at 2–2.5 m, while legs of standing people at the bottom edge are 4–6 m away. In frame 3, as the camera rotates rightward across the terrace, a standing person in a red skirt and white shirt (rendered upside-down in image coordinates) is prominent in the right foreground at roughly 2–2.5 m with their torso and hips facing the camera wearer, while several other people stand along the railing 4–8 m behind and to the left of them. In frames 4 and 5, the camera wearer moves near a bright overhanging structural beam on the upper-left (within 1–1.5 m in frame 4) and retreats or pitches away in frame 5, placing a group of three to four standing and seated people 3–5 m away below/in front of the camera, spaced 0.5–1.5 m apart from one another, with a partially visible person in the upper-right of frame 4 within ~1 m (arm's reach). Compared to RGB alone, the depth map makes the continuous ground-plane gradient, the close overhang clearance in frame 4, and the depth separation between foreground figures and background trees immediately apparent, though it is unreliable along the top-down ground plane where the floor appears almost as bright as elevated objects and where cast shadows and sky/foliage boundaries blur depth discontinuities.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates only a small fraction of the scene's occupants and furniture across the five frames, leaving the tiled floor, railing, building overhang, and most people unsegmented in black. In frames 1 and 2, it segments the seated person in the upper-left at 1.5–2 m (facing sideways to the right and looking down at their own feet within their arm's reach) and partially segments the legs of people standing 4–6 m away at the bottom edge, plus a person on the far left of frame 3 at ~3–4 m. In frame 4, it detects only the partially visible person at the upper-right edge within ~1 m (arm's reach of the camera wearer) and one standing person at ~3.5 m, while frame 5 is completely empty with zero masks. While segmentation helps confirm the boundary of the seated person's crouched profile and flags truncated figures at the frame borders that are easy to overlook in RGB, it is highly unreliable due to the upside-down camera orientation. Specifically, it misclassifies the large white oval planter/bench and surrounding floor on the left of frame 1 as a 'toilet', and completely fails to detect the central standing person at 2 m in frame 3 as well as the entire group of people 3–5 m away in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map tracks skeletal keypoints for selected individuals across the strip, helping disambiguate body and limb orientations despite the inverted camera perspective. In frame 1, a partial yellow skeleton on the upper-left marks the head and shoulders of the seated person at 1.5–2 m leaning rightward toward their feet, while frame 2 loses their body skeleton entirely and instead renders only magenta hand keypoints where their outstretched hands touch their shoes (within their own arm's reach, ~1.5–2 m from the camera wearer). In frame 3, a full yellow body skeleton captures the upside-down standing person at 2–2.5 m with hands on hips and torso facing toward the camera wearer, and in frames 4 and 5, yellow skeletons track one standing person (frame 4, ~3.5 m) and the central red-skirted person (frame 5, ~3.5–4 m) facing generally toward the camera wearer as the distance between them increases. The pose map makes exact limb articulation—such as the seated person's two hands aligned at their ankles in frame 2 and the bent-elbow, hands-on-hips posture in frames 3 and 5—easier to parse than in the wide-angle RGB, especially against cluttered shadows. However, it is unreliable across the sequence because the inverted orientation causes frequent missed detections, dropping the seated person's torso in frame 2, missing the close partial person at <1 m in frame 4, and failing to detect all other nearby standing and seated people 3–8 m away.
